Party pooper
PAR-tee POO-per
noun (Silent Generation slang)
American slang recorded from the early 1950s for someone who spoils the fun or leaves a party early; pooper comes from the older slang poop out, to tire out or quit, so the first party pooper was the one too tired to keep going. Party came into English from French partie, a part or side, and Webster in 1828 defined it first as a faction and only sixth as "a select company invited to an entertainment."

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1953, the party pooper was the fellow who yawned at nine o’clock, wanted the music turned down, or went home before the cake. Nobody wanted to be one. Scripture has a surprising amount to say on both sides. First, God is not a party pooper. The Lord Jesus did His first miracle at a wedding feast in Cana, turning water into wine so the celebration would not end in shame. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22), and there is "a time to laugh… and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4). Christians are told to "Rejoice with them that do rejoice" (Rom 12:15), which means a sour face at a friend’s happy day is a small failure of love. But there is another side. Some parties ought to be left early. "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" (Pro 1:10). The believer who walks out of the wrong kind of party will be called worse names than party pooper: "they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you" (1Pe 4:4). Grandchildren, be the first to laugh at a good feast and the first to leave a wicked one. The Lord who made the wine at Cana will one day sit with His people at the marriage supper of the Lamb — the best feast there will ever be.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (early 1950s American) for a killjoy who spoils the fun — though Scripture says there is a time to laugh and a time to refuse: My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not (Pro 1:10).

PARTY POOPER, n. (Silent Generation slang, early 1950s; from poop out, to tire and quit) A killjoy; one who spoils the fun or leaves a party early. "Don’t be a party pooper — stay for one more song."

Webster (1828) — PARTY, noun [Latin pars. See Part .] 1. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community. 6. A select company invited to an entertainment; as a dining party a tea party an evening party

Decode for families: a killjoy; laugh at the good feast, and leave the wicked one.

Key Scripture

Pro 17:22 — "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones."

Ecc 3:4 — "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;"

Rom 12:15 — "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."

Pro 1:10 — "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not."

1Pe 4:4 — "Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:"

Modern Corruption

A playful word that is usually harmless, but the fear of being called one has pushed many young people to stay at parties they should have left.

expand to see more

A genuine killjoy — the one who sulks at every celebration — does deserve a gentle nudge. Joy at a wedding, a birthday or a homecoming is right, and Scripture commands it.

The word does its real damage as a weapon. It shames the one who says no, and it has kept many a teenager at a party long after the drinking started. Teach children that the name is cheap and their conscience is not; Christ will honour the one who walked out.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

French partie (a part, a side) → party (a company; later, a social gathering) + poop out (to tire, quit) → early-1950s party pooper.
